overview: Ho-Chunk homelands center on what is now Wisconsin and surrounding parts of the upper Midwest. The imported map is a broad regional outline, not a kingdom’s surveyed frontier, and its 1492 to 1500 interval is only map coverage. Today the Ho-Chunk Nation in Wisconsin and the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska are distinct governments with a shared people’s history.

periods.title: Homelands and village life
periods.summary: Gardens, waterways and community relationships supported life in the upper Midwest.

periods.title: Trade and changing alliances
periods.summary: European contact, colonial competition and expanding settlement brought new pressures and choices.

periods.title: Removal and return
periods.summary: Successive forced relocations scattered families; many kept returning to Wisconsin.

periods.title: Continuing communities
periods.summary: Ho-Chunk people maintained communities in Wisconsin and Nebraska and developed their own modern institutions.

items.text: Ho-Chunk oral tradition describes an enduring relationship with the homeland. The Nation’s own account names Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri and Illinois among its traditional lands. This community account gives a larger setting than the outline on this map and connects present generations with places important to their ancestors.

Gardens supplied corn, beans and other foods that could be dried for winter. The Milwaukee Public Museum describes storage in fiber bags and underground pits. A good harvest had to be followed by good storage: growing dinner was only the first half of keeping it available in January.

Dugout canoes helped people travel up the Fox and Wisconsin rivers on hunting journeys. The museum account describes leaving the canoes in a protected place when travelers continued overland. Boats, walking routes and knowledge of seasonal resources worked together across a landscape much larger than a single village.

Clans linked relatives and carried responsibilities. In the museum’s account, Ho-Chunk clan relatives helped provide children’s names; Thunderbird people had peacekeeping duties and Bear people had policing responsibilities. A family connection could therefore also tell someone what work they owed the wider community.

Black ash basket making could involve an entire family. The Museum of Wisconsin Art describes men preparing wood strips and carving handles, while women commonly dyed and wove the strips. Techniques and preferred colors passed between generations. Making the container began in the forest, well before anyone started weaving.

Roadside basket stands connected Ho-Chunk households with travelers through Wisconsin. Museum researchers found sales records listing prices for different basket types. These were artworks and useful goods, but also family income that helped people remain together while outside policies repeatedly disrupted their lives.

One surviving basket has a named maker: Alvina Foss, also known as Alvina Miner or Alvina Yellowthunder. The Smithsonian dates her Wisconsin Ho-Chunk basket to 1990 to 2000 and lists ash splints, wood and synthetic dyes. Its record preserves an individual artist within a much longer family tradition.

The Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska’s language and culture program reported growing a garden with corn, beans, squash and a fourth companion, sunflower. Its 2021 account describes students and volunteers helping, with harvests shared at community gatherings and funerals. Gardening could feed people and create opportunities to work beside one another.

In fiscal 2025, the Ho-Chunk Nation’s agriculture department reported a produce-box pilot with 29 participants. Radishes from its fields also entered the Tribal Elder Food Box Program. These are recent examples of tribal farming linking growers, households and elders through an organized food supply.

sections.title: Political upheaval and a living voice

items.text: Jean Nicolet met Ho-Chunk people in 1634 during French efforts to build western trade relationships. The precise meeting place is disputed, and the written account was produced years later. The encounter belonged to a world of Indigenous alliances and choices that Europeans were trying to enter.

Nineteenth-century United States policies repeatedly forced Ho-Chunk families westward through Iowa, Minnesota and South Dakota. Many returned to Wisconsin; others established a lasting home in Nebraska, where a reservation was created in 1865. The two present governments reflect this history of forced movement and persistence.

Wisconsin families combined their own gardens with seasonal paid work picking crops such as strawberries, cherries and cranberries. They returned home between jobs to tend their food plots. The museum describes an economy built from several kinds of work, rather than a single job that stayed the same all year.

HoChunk Renaissance in Nebraska rebuilt its teaching approach in 2003 around teams: a fluent speaker, an apprentice and a support worker. Classes reached settings from daycare to college. The apprentice could learn while helping teach, creating a path toward another generation of language teachers.

The Ho-Chunk Nation’s official website greets visitors with “Hocąk Wazijacira Hižąkiišąną Hįįnį Karagiwiną”, translated there as “The Ho-Chunk Nation greets each and every one of you”. This is the Nation’s own modern written welcome, with its spelling preserved here.

The Wisconsin Ho-Chunk Nation describes separate executive, legislative and judicial branches, along with its General Council. Its courts include a Traditional Court as well as other judicial institutions. Modern self-government can therefore hold elected administration and community traditions within the same political system.

ending.text: The map ends in 1500, but Ho-Chunk history continues through removal, return and institution building. The Ho-Chunk Nation and Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska remain separate sovereign governments. Families, artists, growers and language teachers continue to shape their communities.
